paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The dream of a machine that could translate between human languages is almost as old as the computer itself. In the years after the Second World War, a handful of researchers, impressed by the success of code-breaking during the conflict, suggested that a text in Russian might be treated as English that had simply been written in a strange code. If the code could be cracked, they reasoned, translation would become a mechanical procedure. The analogy was attractive, but it rested on a profound misunderstanding of what languages are, and it would take more than half a century, and several complete changes of approach, before machines could produce translations that people were genuinely willing to read.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Early optimism appeared to be justified by a public demonstration in 1954, in which a computer translated around sixty carefully selected Russian sentences into English. Newspapers reported that fully automatic translation was only a few years away, and government funding followed. The system, however, knew only about 250 words and six grammatical rules, and the sentences had been chosen precisely because they could be handled by such a limited program. Over the following decade, researchers discovered that every apparent advance revealed new and more stubborn difficulties, from words with several meanings to sentences whose structure could only be understood with knowledge of the world.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: By the mid-1960s, patience was running out. A committee appointed to advise the United States government concluded in 1966 that machine translation was slower, less accurate and more expensive than human translation, and that there was no immediate prospect of useful results. Funding was cut dramatically, and for many years the field was regarded with suspicion by scientists and officials alike. Work did not stop altogether, however. Smaller projects continued, particularly in Canada and Europe, where the practical need to translate large volumes of official documents between several languages kept interest alive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These systems, like their predecessors, were based on rules. Teams of linguists wrote detailed descriptions of the grammar of each language and compiled enormous bilingual dictionaries, and programmers turned these into instructions that the computer could follow. The approach could work well in narrow fields with predictable language, such as weather forecasts, but it was extremely costly to build and maintain. Every new pair of languages required years of expert labour, and the rules frequently conflicted with one another when faced with the endless variety of real texts. Human language, it turned out, contains far more exceptions than any team could list.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A fundamentally different idea emerged at the end of the 1980s. Instead of telling the computer how languages work, researchers allowed it to discover patterns for itself by analysing very large collections of texts that had already been translated by humans, such as the proceedings of bilingual parliaments. These statistical systems calculated which words and phrases in one language most often corresponded to which in another, and chose the most probable translation for each new sentence. They required no knowledge of grammar, which some linguists found disturbing, but they improved steadily as more data became available, and by the early 2000s they had largely replaced rule-based methods.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The most recent change came in the middle of the 2010s with the arrival of neural machine translation. These systems use networks of artificial 'neurons', loosely modelled on the brain, which process a whole sentence at once rather than breaking it into fragments. The resulting translations are noticeably more fluent, and on some measures the quality of output between widely used language pairs improved more in a few years than it had in the previous decade. Neural systems are now used by hundreds of millions of people every day, often without any awareness that a machine is involved, for instance when a website is displayed automatically in the reader's own language.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Yet it would be wrong to conclude that the problem has been solved. Neural systems still struggle with languages for which little translated text exists, and they can produce sentences that are perfectly fluent but entirely wrong, a weakness that is particularly dangerous because readers have no obvious signal that something has gone astray. They also reproduce biases present in their training data, for example by assuming that doctors are male and nurses female. For these reasons, professional translators increasingly work alongside machines rather than being replaced by them, correcting and refining output rather than starting from a blank page. The original dream of fully automatic, high-quality translation remains, for many purposes, a dream.

title: The Wood Wide Web: Do Trees Really Share?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Beneath the floor of almost every forest lies a vast network of fine threads. These are the hyphae of fungi, many of which live in close partnership with the roots of trees. In this relationship, known as a mycorrhiza, the fungus supplies the tree with water and with nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which it is able to extract from the soil far more efficiently than roots can. In return, the tree provides the fungus with sugars produced by photosynthesis. The arrangement is ancient: fossil evidence suggests that partnerships of this kind helped the first plants to colonise dry land some 400 million years ago.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Because a single fungus can connect with the roots of several trees, and a single tree can host many fungi, scientists have long suspected that these partnerships might link whole groups of trees together. In the late 1990s, a study in a Canadian forest appeared to confirm this. Researchers supplied young trees of two different species with carbon in a form that could be traced, and later detected some of it in neighbouring trees. The results, published in a leading scientific journal, were presented to the public under the memorable label of the 'wood wide web', and the idea that trees use fungal networks to exchange resources quickly spread far beyond the scientific community.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In the years that followed, the concept grew considerably more ambitious. Popular books, documentaries and newspaper articles described large 'mother trees' that recognise their own offspring and send them food through the network, and forests in which trees warn each other of insect attacks by means of chemical signals. Some accounts suggested that forests should be understood less as collections of competing individuals than as cooperative communities. These ideas proved enormously appealing, partly because they offered a hopeful vision of nature at a time of widespread anxiety about the environment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Recently, however, a number of researchers have argued that public enthusiasm has run well ahead of the evidence. A detailed review published in 2023 re-examined the field studies most often cited in support of the theory and concluded that many of them had been interpreted too generously. In several cases, the experiments could not rule out the possibility that resources had travelled between trees through the soil itself rather than through fungal threads. In others, the amount of carbon transferred was so small that it was unlikely to make any meaningful difference to the receiving tree. The authors were careful to say that networks exist; what they questioned was the claim that these networks play a major role in the life of forests.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In my view, this criticism is both justified and healthy. Field research on underground networks is extremely difficult. Fungal threads are far thinner than a human hair, they break easily when soil is disturbed, and a single handful of earth may contain dozens of species. Proving that a particular substance moved from one tree to another through a particular fungus, rather than by some other route, requires experiments of great precision, and such experiments have rarely been carried out in mature forests rather than in containers or among seedlings. It is not surprising that early results were open to more than one interpretation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What concerns me more is the way in which uncertain findings were transformed into confident statements as they passed from scientific journals to the wider public. Researchers themselves were not always responsible for this; journalists and authors often simplified or exaggerated their conclusions. Nevertheless, the episode shows how easily a striking metaphor can take on a life of its own. Once the image of trees sharing food and messages had become familiar, it was frequently repeated as established fact, and the more cautious language of the original studies was lost.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that mycorrhizal fungi are unimportant. On the contrary, their role in supplying trees with water and nutrients is firmly established, and forestry practices that damage soil fungi can seriously harm the growth of new trees. The open questions concern the extent to which networks connect trees in the wild and whether those connections benefit the forest as a whole. Answering them will require patient, carefully designed research. In the meantime, it would be wise to treat the most dramatic claims about the wood wide web as interesting possibilities rather than settled science.
